descs.t: Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged with two counts under the Espionage Act for allegedly leaking national defense information to a reporter in 2016. It is the third time the Justice Department has charged him in little more than a year, his attorney Pat Fitzgerald says. We walk through what the charges allege and what happens next.

James Comey now faces Espionage Act charges, accused of transmitting and conspiring to transmit national defense information to the press in 2016. The Justice Department filed the charges to stop the statute of limitations from running out, and Comey's lawyer calls it the third case in a year. We look at the counts, the timing and the defense.

The former head of the FBI is charged under the Espionage Act, accused of leaking national defense information to a reporter in 2016. It is the third case against James Comey in little more than a year. We lay out what he is accused of, why the timing matters, and whether this case can stick.

intro.plain: Big legal news out of Washington. Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged under the Espionage Act, two counts, accused of leaking national defense information to a reporter back in 2016. His lawyer says this is the third time the Justice Department has charged him in little more than a year. Chat, tell me: do you think this one goes to trial?
intro.mid: James Comey is charged again, and this time it is the Espionage Act. The Justice Department says he leaked national defense information to a reporter in 2016, and it filed now to stop the statute of limitations from running out. His lawyer calls it the third case in a year. Chat, is this accountability or a pattern of going after him?
intro.bold: Third time. James Comey, the man who ran the FBI, is now charged under the Espionage Act, accused of leaking national defense information to the press in 2016. The Justice Department filed before the legal clock ran out, and his lawyer is already firing back. Chat, straight question: should a former FBI director face trial for this?

descs.t: Israelis are voting on whether to keep Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister after three years of war. Betting odds on him staying fell to a record low as centrist former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot surged. We walk through the race, the main challenger and the outcomes on the table.

Benjamin Netanyahu faces Gadi Eisenkot, the former IDF chief who calls him delusional and says Iran did not have nuclear weapons, as Israel votes. The New York Times reports officials say Netanyahu pushed for an attack on Iran before the election, and some say he could lose and still stay in power. We look at every path from here.

After three years of war, Israel votes on Benjamin Netanyahu, the leader President Trump has endorsed. His challenger Gadi Eisenkot claims Iran had no nuclear weapons, a claim that goes to the heart of the war. We lay out what is at stake for Israel, for its fight with Iran's regime, and for the next government.

intro.plain: Israel is voting today, and the question is simple: does Benjamin Netanyahu stay after three years of war? Betting odds on him staying just hit a record low, with former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot surging. Polls in Israel have missed before, so nothing is settled. Chat, tell me: does Netanyahu hold on or not?
intro.mid: Election day in Israel. Gadi Eisenkot, the former IDF chief, is calling Netanyahu delusional and saying Iran did not have nuclear weapons. The New York Times reports officials say Netanyahu pushed for an attack on Iran before the vote. And some say he could lose and still stay prime minister. Chat, what do you make of Eisenkot's claim about Iran?
intro.bold: Three years of war, and today Israelis decide whether Benjamin Netanyahu keeps his job. Trump has endorsed him. His challenger Gadi Eisenkot says Iran had no nuclear weapons, which goes straight to why this war was fought. If Netanyahu falls, Iran's regime will be watching who replaces him. Chat, straight question: who should lead Israel now?

hook.plain: Israelis are voting on Benjamin Netanyahu after three years of war, and his odds just hit a record low. Here is the race and how it could end.

hook.bold: Three years of war, one vote. Netanyahu's odds are at a record low and his challenger is questioning the case on Iran. Here is what Israel decides today.

descs.t: Lula da Silva has won Brazil's presidential runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro. A day later, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports, and Bolsonaro has since withdrawn his legal challenge and says he will sue Lula for abuse of power. We walk through the result, the passport order and what Trump has said about it.

Lula's comeback in Brazil is the first time since 1985 that a candidate who lost the first round went on to win the runoff, according to The Economist. Reuters commentary calls it a harsh blow to Trump's Donroe Doctrine, while Trump says he likes Lula and is not running Brazil. We look at what the result and the passport order against Flávio Bolsonaro mean for Trump's plans in the region.

Flávio Bolsonaro lost Brazil's runoff to Lula and was ordered to give up his passports the very next day, by order of Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Voices on the right are calling the vote stolen, and Flávio has dropped his challenge. We ask what the passport order tells us about where Brazil is heading.

descs.t: Serbia's Student List has won Sunday's snap election, ending the 12-year rule of pro-Russian strongman Vucic, with record turnout and a projected 140 of 250 seats. We go through the result and how the students got here.

A student-led movement has ousted Vucic in Serbia peacefully, and is projected to win about 140 of 250 seats. Supporters gathered at Slavija Square in Belgrade, and Serbia now waits to learn how the new leaders will govern. We look at the win, what it means for Russia's influence and the tests ahead.

No fires, no looting, record turnout: Serbia's students voted a 12-year strongman out of power. We walk through how a peaceful movement beat a pro-Russian regime at the ballot box, and why every opposition facing a dictatorship should be watching.

intro.plain: Big result out of Serbia. The Student List won Sunday's snap election and ended Vucic's 12 years in power, with record turnout and about 140 of 250 seats projected. Supporters packed Slavija Square in Belgrade. Chat, did you see this coming?
